text: As far as the east is from the west, so far hath he removed our transgressions from us.
reflection: If you travel north, eventually you reach the North Pole and begin heading south. North and south meet. But east and west never do. You can travel east forever and never start going west. David may not have known all the geography, but he chose his picture well: "As far as the east is from the west, so far hath he removed our transgressions from us." God does not move our sins a short distance away, where we might stumble over them again. He removes them completely, to a distance that cannot be measured. Many people believe God forgives them, yet still carry the weight of old failures. They replay past mistakes and feel condemned. But if God has removed your sin that far, you do not need to go looking for it. This month we will think about forgiveness, both receiving it and giving it. Begin by receiving it fully. Let what God has removed stay removed.
question: What forgiven sin have you been carrying again that God has already removed?
prayer: Lord, You have removed my transgressions as far as the east is from the west. Help me receive Your forgiveness fully, and let what You have removed stay removed. Amen.

text: Blessed is he whose transgression is forgiven, whose sin is covered.
reflection: David knew the weight of sin. Psalm 32 describes what it felt like before he confessed: his bones wasted away, he groaned all day long, and God's hand was heavy on him. Hidden sin had drained the life out of him. So when he finally experienced forgiveness, he burst into this declaration: "Blessed is he whose transgression is forgiven, whose sin is covered." Blessed means deeply happy, truly well off. Real happiness is not found in never having failed. It is found in being forgiven. Covered is a beautiful word. It pictures God placing a covering over our sin so that it is no longer exposed before Him. We do not cover it ourselves. That only leads to hiding and heaviness. God covers it, and that brings freedom. If you are carrying something you have never brought to God, the weight does not have to stay. The joy of being forgiven is waiting on the other side of honesty.
question: Is there anything hidden you could bring to God today so you can know the joy of forgiveness?
prayer: Lord, blessed is the one whose sin is forgiven and covered. I bring You what I have kept hidden, and I ask You to give me the joy of being forgiven. Amen.

text: I acknowledged my sin unto thee, and mine iniquity have I not hid. I said, I will confess my transgressions unto the LORD; and thou forgavest the iniquity of my sin. Selah.
reflection: Later in Psalm 32, David tells exactly how his freedom came: "I acknowledged my sin unto thee, and mine iniquity have I not hid. I said, I will confess my transgressions unto the LORD; and thou forgavest the iniquity of my sin." Notice the simplicity. David stopped hiding. He acknowledged what he had done. He did not make excuses, shift blame, or minimize. He confessed. And God forgave. Confession is not about informing God of something He does not know. He already knows. It is about agreeing with Him, being honest about our sin rather than defending it. Confession clears the air between us and God. It ends the exhausting work of hiding. Many of us delay confession because we fear what will happen. But David discovered that on the other side of confession was not condemnation but forgiveness. Is there something you have been hiding from God? You do not need to keep carrying it. Say it plainly to Him today. He is ready to forgive.
question: What have you been hiding from God that you could honestly confess to Him today?
prayer: Lord, I stop hiding and acknowledge my sin to You. Thank You that You forgive the iniquity of my sin. Free me from the weight of keeping secrets from You. Amen.

text: Come now, and let us reason together, saith the LORD: though your sins be as scarlet, they shall be as white as snow; though they be red like crimson, they shall be as wool.
reflection: God's people had wandered far from Him. Isaiah's opening chapter describes their rebellion in painful detail. Yet in the middle of the charges, God extends an invitation: "Come now, and let us reason together, saith the LORD: though your sins be as scarlet, they shall be as white as snow." Scarlet dye was one of the most permanent colours in the ancient world. Once a cloth was dyed scarlet, it was almost impossible to make it white again. That is a picture of sin's stain. We cannot scrub it out ourselves. But God can. He promises to make what is deeply stained as white as fresh snow and clean wool. Notice that the invitation comes first: come now. God does not wait for us to clean ourselves before we approach Him. He invites us to come as we are, stains and all, and let Him do the cleansing. Whatever stain you feel today, accept His invitation. Come now.
question: What stain do you feel you cannot remove, and could you bring it to God as you are today?
prayer: Lord, You invite me to come and reason with You. Though my sins be as scarlet, You can make them white as snow. I come to You just as I am. Amen.

text: Who is a God like unto thee, that pardoneth iniquity, and passeth by the transgression of the remnant of his heritage? he retaineth not his anger for ever, because he delighteth in mercy.
reflection: The prophet Micah's name means Who is like the Lord? He ends his book by answering his own name with wonder: "Who is a God like unto thee, that pardoneth iniquity, and passeth by the transgression of the remnant of his heritage?" There is no other god like this. The idols of the nations around Israel were feared for their anger and demanded endless appeasement. But the true God is different. He pardons. He passes over transgression. And the reason is stunning: "he retaineth not his anger for ever, because he delighteth in mercy." God does not forgive reluctantly, as though it costs Him to be kind. He delights in mercy. It brings Him joy. This changes how we approach Him. We do not have to beg a reluctant God. We come to a Father who is glad to forgive. If you have been afraid to come to God because of your failures, remember this verse. He delights in mercy. Come and let Him enjoy forgiving you.
question: Do you approach God as if He forgives reluctantly, and how would it change things to know He delights in mercy?
prayer: Lord, who is a God like You, who pardons iniquity and delights in mercy? Thank You that You are glad to forgive. I come to You today with confidence. Amen.

text: He will turn again, he will have compassion upon us; he will subdue our iniquities; and thou wilt cast all their sins into the depths of the sea.
reflection: Micah continues his song of wonder with three vivid promises: "He will turn again, he will have compassion upon us; he will subdue our iniquities; and thou wilt cast all their sins into the depths of the sea." First, God turns again toward us with compassion. He does not keep His face turned away. Second, He subdues our iniquities. He does not only forgive sin; He also defeats its power over us. And third, He casts our sins into the depths of the sea. In the ancient world, the deep sea was the most unreachable place imaginable. Whatever sank there was gone for good. That is where God sends our sins. Not into a drawer where He can pull them out later, but into depths that cannot be reached. Some people like to say that God then puts up a sign: no fishing allowed. Do not go diving for what God has buried. If He has cast it into the sea, leave it there.
question: Is there a sin God has buried that you keep going back to dig up?
prayer: Lord, You have cast my sins into the depths of the sea. Help me stop searching for what You have buried, and let me walk away from it in freedom. Amen.

text: And forgive us our debts, as we forgive our debtors.
reflection: When Jesus taught His disciples to pray, He included a line that is easy to say but hard to live: "And forgive us our debts, as we forgive our debtors." Sin is pictured as a debt, something we owe and cannot repay. We ask God to cancel what we owe Him. But in the same breath, we commit to canceling what others owe us. The two are tied together. A heart that has truly received mercy becomes a merciful heart. It would be strange to ask God to forgive a mountain of debt while we refuse to forgive a few coins owed to us. Jesus later told a parable about exactly that. Praying this line honestly can be uncomfortable. It brings to mind the people who have hurt us. But that discomfort can lead to freedom. Today, as you ask God for forgiveness, ask Him also for the grace to forgive. Name the person in your heart. Release the debt as He has released yours.
question: Whose debt against you could you ask God for grace to release today?
prayer: Father, forgive me my debts, as I forgive my debtors. You have shown me such mercy; make my heart merciful too, and help me release what I am owed. Amen.

text: For if ye forgive men their trespasses, your heavenly Father will also forgive you…
reflection: Right after teaching His disciples to pray, Jesus returned to one line and explained it further: "For if ye forgive men their trespasses, your heavenly Father will also forgive you." Of all the lines in the prayer, this is the one He chose to emphasize. Forgiveness matters deeply to God. This does not mean we earn God's forgiveness by forgiving others. Salvation is a gift of grace. But a heart that refuses to forgive shows that it has not truly grasped how much it has been forgiven. Unforgiveness also harms us. It keeps old wounds open and ties us to the people who hurt us. Bitterness grows in its soil. Forgiving does not mean pretending the wrong was small, or that trust is immediately restored. It means releasing the debt to God and refusing to hold it over the other person. It is usually a journey rather than one decision. Today, take one step on that path. Ask God to help you forgive.
question: Who is one person you could take a step toward forgiving today?
prayer: Father, You have forgiven me so much. Where unforgiveness has taken root in me, soften my heart, and help me take one step toward forgiving today. Amen.

text: Then came Peter to him, and said, Lord, how oft shall my brother sin against me, and I forgive him? till seven times?
reflection: Peter thought he was being generous. Jewish teachers of the time suggested forgiving someone three times. So Peter more than doubled it: "Lord, how oft shall my brother sin against me, and I forgive him? till seven times?" Seven was a number of completeness. Surely forgiving someone seven times for the same kind of offence was more than enough. Peter's question is very human. We want to know where the limit is. At what point can we stop forgiving and start protecting ourselves? When does patience run out? It is an honest question, especially when someone keeps hurting us. Notice that Peter is asking about a brother, someone close to him. Repeated hurts often come from the people nearest to us: family members, friends, coworkers. Those wounds can feel the deepest. If you have been counting someone's offences, you are not alone. Peter did too. Bring your count to Jesus today and listen for His answer. We will hear it tomorrow.
question: Is there someone you have been keeping count with, waiting to stop forgiving?
prayer: Lord Jesus, like Peter, I want to know where forgiveness can stop. I bring You my count of offences. Teach me the forgiveness that does not keep a tally. Amen.

text: Jesus saith unto him, I say not unto thee, Until seven times: but, Until seventy times seven.
reflection: Jesus answered Peter's question with a number that stopped counting altogether: "I say not unto thee, Until seven times: but, Until seventy times seven." Four hundred and ninety. But Jesus was not giving Peter a new limit to track. He was saying, stop keeping score. Forgiveness is not a ledger with a final line. Then Jesus told a story about a servant who was forgiven a debt he could never repay, millions in today's terms. Yet that same servant refused to forgive another servant whose debt to him was tiny. The master was outraged. The point was clear. When we grasp how much God has forgiven us, our small debts against others look different. This does not mean we allow ourselves to be endlessly abused. Forgiveness and boundaries can go together. But it does mean we do not run out of grace. Today, put away the scorecard. Let God's limitless forgiveness of you shape your forgiveness of others.
question: What scorecard against someone could you put away today?
prayer: Lord Jesus, You told me to forgive until seventy times seven. When I remember how much You have forgiven me, help me put away my scorecard for good. Amen.

text: Judge not, and ye shall not be judged: condemn not, and ye shall not be condemned: forgive, and ye shall be forgiven…
reflection: Jesus gave a series of short commands about how we treat others: "Judge not, and ye shall not be judged: condemn not, and ye shall not be condemned: forgive, and ye shall be forgiven." It is easy to become a harsh judge of others. We see their faults clearly while overlooking our own. We assume the worst about their motives. We decide what they deserve. Jesus is not saying we should never discern right from wrong. Elsewhere He tells us to judge rightly. He is warning against a critical, condemning spirit that sets itself up above others. That kind of spirit tends to come back on us. People who are quick to condemn often find themselves condemned. But people who are generous with mercy tend to receive it. The verse goes on to say, give, and it shall be given unto you. The measure we use for others is the measure we receive. Today, choose mercy over judgment. Look for the good in others and be quick to forgive.
question: Where could you choose mercy over judgment today?
prayer: Lord Jesus, keep me from a critical and condemning spirit. Teach me to forgive freely and to measure others with the same mercy You have shown me. Amen.

text: And he arose, and came to his father. But when he was yet a great way off, his father saw him, and had compassion, and ran, and fell on his neck, and kissed him.
reflection: The younger son had demanded his inheritance, left home, and wasted everything in reckless living. Now, starving and ashamed, he was walking home with a speech prepared. He would ask to be treated as a hired servant. But something happened before he could even begin: "when he was yet a great way off, his father saw him, and had compassion, and ran, and fell on his neck, and kissed him." The father saw him a great way off. He must have been watching the road. He had compassion. And he ran. In that culture, an older man running was considered undignified. But this father did not care about his dignity. He cared about his son. This is Jesus' picture of God. Not a stern judge waiting for us to grovel, but a Father watching the road, ready to run. If you have wandered, the way home is open. Take the first step, and you may find Him already running toward you.
question: If you have wandered from God, what step toward home could you take today?
prayer: Father, You saw the prodigal from far off and ran to meet him. If I have wandered, help me turn toward home, knowing You are eager to welcome me. Amen.

text: For this my son was dead, and is alive again; he was lost, and is found. And they began to be merry.
reflection: The father in Jesus' story did not just welcome his son home. He threw a party. He called for the best robe, a ring, shoes, and a feast. And he explained why: "For this my son was dead, and is alive again; he was lost, and is found." To the father, it was as if his son had come back to life. The son had been lost, and now he was found. That was worth celebrating. Not everyone was happy. The older brother was angry and refused to join the party. He felt his faithfulness had gone unnoticed while his brother's rebellion was rewarded. His reaction warns us. It is possible to be close to the Father's house and still miss the Father's heart. God rejoices when the lost come home. Do we rejoice too, or do we resent the grace shown to others? Today, celebrate the return of anyone who has come back to God. And if you are the one who was lost, know that heaven is celebrating you.
question: Is there grace shown to someone else that you have resented, and could you rejoice in it instead?
prayer: Father, You rejoice over every one who comes home. Free me from the older brother's resentment, and help me rejoice in grace shown to others, as heaven rejoices over me. Amen.

text: But as for you, ye thought evil against me; but God meant it unto good, to bring to pass, as it is this day, to save much people alive.
reflection: Joseph's brothers had sold him into slavery out of jealousy. He spent years as a slave and a prisoner in Egypt. But God raised him up to become second in command over the whole land, and through his wisdom, many lives were saved during a terrible famine. After their father died, the brothers feared Joseph would finally take revenge. Instead, he said, "ye thought evil against me; but God meant it unto good, to bring to pass, as it is this day, to save much people alive." Joseph did not deny the evil. He named it plainly. But he saw a bigger story. God had taken their evil intentions and woven them into a plan to save many lives. This perspective is what allowed Joseph to forgive. He did not need revenge because he trusted God's purpose. When people have wronged you, it can be hard to see any good. But God is still at work. He can bring purpose out of pain. Trust Him with the story.
question: What wrong done to you could you trust God to bring good out of?
prayer: Lord, what others meant for evil, You can mean for good. Help me trust Your purpose in the wrongs done to me, and give me a heart that forgives instead of seeking revenge. Amen.

text: Now therefore be not grieved, nor angry with yourselves, that ye sold me hither: for God did send me before you to preserve life.
reflection: This was the moment Joseph revealed himself to his brothers. For years they had carried the guilt of what they had done. Now they stood before the powerful governor of Egypt, terrified, as he told them he was the brother they had sold. They expected punishment. Instead Joseph said, "be not grieved, nor angry with yourselves, that ye sold me hither: for God did send me before you to preserve life." Joseph not only forgave his brothers. He comforted them. He told them not to be consumed by guilt. He pointed them to God's purpose. This is forgiveness at its most beautiful. It does not just release the offender from punishment. It seeks their healing and restoration. It reaches across the hurt with compassion. Joseph wept as he embraced them. Forgiveness like this is a gift of God's grace. We cannot manufacture it on our own. But God can grow it in us. Ask Him today for a heart like Joseph's.
question: Is there someone whose healing you could seek as you forgive them, as Joseph did?
prayer: Lord, give me a heart that forgives like Joseph's, one that seeks the healing of those who hurt me, not just their release. Show me Your purpose in my story. Amen.

text: And Esau ran to meet him, and embraced him, and fell on his neck, and kissed him: and they wept.
reflection: Twenty years earlier, Jacob had cheated his brother Esau out of their father's blessing. Esau was so angry that he planned to kill him, and Jacob fled for his life. Now, after many years away, Jacob was returning home. He heard that Esau was coming to meet him with four hundred men. Jacob was terrified. He prayed, sent gifts ahead, and bowed to the ground seven times as he approached. But then "Esau ran to meet him, and embraced him, and fell on his neck, and kissed him: and they wept." The feared confrontation became a reunion. Esau's anger had softened over the years, and God had been at work in both brothers' hearts. Some relationships feel permanently broken. Years of silence or conflict can make reconciliation seem impossible. But God can soften hearts, including ours. If there is a broken relationship in your life, pray for it today. The reunion you fear may become the embrace you long for.
question: Which broken relationship in your life could you pray for today?
prayer: Lord, You softened the hearts of Jacob and Esau after many years. I bring You a broken relationship in my life. Soften our hearts, and bring reconciliation in Your time. Amen.

text: Leave there thy gift before the altar, and go thy way; first be reconciled to thy brother, and then come and offer thy gift.
reflection: In the Sermon on the Mount, Jesus described a man bringing an offering to the altar. As he stood there, he remembered that his brother had something against him. What should he do? Jesus said, "Leave there thy gift before the altar, and go thy way; first be reconciled to thy brother, and then come and offer thy gift." This is startling. Jesus says that making peace with a brother is so important that worship can wait. God does not want our offerings while we ignore broken relationships. Our relationship with Him and our relationships with others are deeply connected. Notice too that the brother has something against the worshipper. Jesus does not ask who is at fault. He simply says, go. Take the first step, even if the other person is the one who is upset. Reconciliation is not always possible; it takes two. But we can do our part. Is there someone you need to make things right with? Go first.
question: Who might have something against you, and what first step toward peace could you take?
prayer: Lord, my relationship with You is bound up with my relationships with others. Show me where I need to make peace, and give me courage to take the first step. Amen.

text: Let all bitterness, and wrath, and anger, and clamour, and evil speaking, be put away from you, with all malice…
reflection: Paul gives a long list of things to get rid of: "Let all bitterness, and wrath, and anger, and clamour, and evil speaking, be put away from you, with all malice." Notice how they build on one another. Bitterness is a settled resentment, an unhealed wound that sours inside. It leads to wrath, an outburst of temper, and anger, a simmering hostility. These spill out as clamour, loud quarrelling, and evil speaking, words that tear others down. And underneath it all is malice, a desire for harm. These things often start small. A hurt is not dealt with. A grudge is nursed. Over time, bitterness takes root and spreads. Paul says put them away. All of them. That is not easy, and it does not happen in one day. But it starts with a decision and a prayer. The very next verse shows the alternative: kindness, tender hearts, and forgiveness. Today, ask God to show you any root of bitterness, and begin to put it away.
question: Is there a root of bitterness growing from an old hurt that God could help you put away?
prayer: Lord, search my heart for any bitterness, anger, or malice. Heal the hurts where it has taken root, and help me put it away, with Your grace. Amen.

text: Forbearing one another, and forgiving one another, if any man have a quarrel against any: even as Christ forgave you, so also do ye.
reflection: Paul gives a simple standard for forgiveness: "even as Christ forgave you, so also do ye." How did Christ forgive us? Completely. He did not forgive only the small sins and hold the big ones against us. Freely. We did not earn it. Before we asked. He made the way while we were still far from Him. At great cost. Forgiveness was not cheap for Him. That is the standard. It is high, and none of us meet it perfectly. But it also gives us the power to forgive. We cannot give what we have not received. The more deeply we understand Christ's forgiveness of us, the more we are able to extend it to others. When forgiving someone feels impossible, do not start by focusing on what they did. Start by remembering what Christ has done for you. Let His forgiveness flow into you until it begins to flow through you. Forgive as you have been forgiven.
question: When forgiving feels impossible, how could remembering Christ's forgiveness of you help?
prayer: Lord Jesus, You forgave me completely, freely, and at great cost. When forgiving others feels impossible, let me start by remembering how You forgave me. Amen.

text: Recompense to no man evil for evil. Provide things honest in the sight of all men.
reflection: When someone hurts us, our instinct is to hurt them back. It feels like justice. But Paul says, "Recompense to no man evil for evil." Recompense means repay. We are not to pay back evil with more evil. Revenge may feel satisfying for a moment, but it only adds more harm to the world. It keeps the cycle going. It also makes us more like the person who wronged us. Paul adds, "Provide things honest in the sight of all men." In other words, live in a way that is honourable, so that even those watching can see your integrity. The world is watching how we respond to mistreatment. Our response can either confirm their cynicism or show them something different. This does not mean we ignore wrongdoing. God is just, and Paul goes on to say that vengeance belongs to Him. We can trust Him to make things right. Today, if someone has treated you badly, refuse the urge to repay. Do what is right instead.
question: Where are you tempted to repay evil for evil, and what good could you choose instead?
prayer: Lord, I leave it to You to make things right. Keep me from repaying evil for evil, and help me do what is honest and good in the sight of all. Amen.

text: If it be possible, as much as lieth in you, live peaceably with all men.
reflection: Paul is realistic in this verse: "If it be possible, as much as lieth in you, live peaceably with all men." He knows that peace is not always possible. Some people refuse it. Some situations cannot be resolved. Paul does not put the entire burden of every relationship on us. But he does put our part on us. As much as lieth in you. As far as it depends on you. That phrase is both freeing and challenging. Freeing, because we are not responsible for other people's choices. If someone refuses peace after we have genuinely sought it, we can rest. Challenging, because we must honestly ask whether we have done everything we can. Have we apologized for our part? Have we let go of pride? Have we reached out, been gentle, and listened? Peace often requires humility. Think of a relationship that is strained right now. Ask yourself, what lies in me to do? Then do it, and leave the rest with God.
question: What part of making peace lies with you today, and what could you leave with God?
prayer: Lord, as much as lies in me, help me live peaceably with all. Show me my part, give me grace to do it, and help me leave the rest with You. Amen.

text: Be not overcome of evil, but overcome evil with good.
reflection: Paul ends Romans 12 with a short, powerful command: "Be not overcome of evil, but overcome evil with good." There are two ways evil can overcome us. One is by hurting us so deeply that we lose hope. The other is by turning us into people who return evil for evil. When someone treats us badly and we respond with bitterness and revenge, evil has won twice. Paul offers a different strategy: overcome evil with good. Respond to cruelty with kindness, to hatred with blessing, to injury with forgiveness. Just before this verse, Paul quotes Proverbs about feeding an enemy who is hungry and giving him drink when he is thirsty. Good is not weakness. It is the most powerful weapon we have. It disarms hostility, surprises enemies, and reflects the heart of God. This is how Jesus overcame evil, and it is how He calls us to live. Today, think of someone who has wronged you. What good could you do for them?
question: What good could you do today for someone who has wronged you?
prayer: Lord, do not let me be overcome of evil. Help me overcome evil with good, and show me one kind thing I can do today for someone who has hurt me. Amen.

text: The discretion of a man deferreth his anger; and it is his glory to pass over a transgression.
reflection: Not every offence needs a confrontation. Proverbs offers a quiet wisdom: "The discretion of a man deferreth his anger; and it is his glory to pass over a transgression." Discretion is good sense, the ability to see a situation clearly. A person with discretion does not explode at every irritation. They slow down their anger. And they recognize that some offences are better simply overlooked. This is not the same as ignoring serious wrongs or abuse. Some things must be addressed. But many daily offences are small. A thoughtless comment, a forgotten promise, a careless mistake. We can choose to make a big deal of them, or we can let them pass. Proverbs says there is glory in letting them pass. It is a sign of strength and maturity, not weakness. Love chooses not to keep a record of every small wrong. Today, when someone irritates or slights you, consider whether it is worth holding onto. You may find glory in letting it go.
question: What minor offence could you choose to let pass today?
prayer: Lord, give me discretion that is slow to anger. Help me see that not every small wrong needs to be answered, and give me grace to let one pass today. Amen.

text: Hatred stirreth up strifes: but love covereth all sins.
reflection: Proverbs often teaches by contrast. Here it sets two forces side by side: "Hatred stirreth up strifes: but love covereth all sins." Hatred stirs. Like someone stirring a pot, it keeps conflict bubbling. It brings up old offences, spreads gossip, and looks for reasons to fight. Hatred is never satisfied with peace. Love, on the other hand, covers. It does not expose every fault or broadcast every failure. It protects the reputation of others. It chooses discretion and grace. This does not mean love hides serious wrong or enables harmful behaviour. It means love does not go looking for fights. It does not delight in others' failures. It is quick to cover with grace rather than quick to expose with criticism. Peter quoted a similar line when he wrote that love shall cover the multitude of sins. Think about how you speak of others when they are not present. Do your words stir up strife, or do they cover with love? Choose love today.
question: How could your words today cover someone with grace instead of stirring up strife?
prayer: Lord, hatred stirs up strife, but love covers all sins. Guard my tongue from exposing others, and let my words cover with grace today. Amen.

text: And all things are of God, who hath reconciled us to himself by Jesus Christ, and hath given to us the ministry of reconciliation…
reflection: Paul begins this passage with a statement that changes everything: "all things are of God, who hath reconciled us to himself by Jesus Christ." Reconciliation means bringing together two parties who were separated. Sin had separated us from God. We could not bridge that gap on our own. So God took the initiative. Through Jesus Christ, He brought us back to Himself. Then Paul adds something surprising. God "hath given to us the ministry of reconciliation." Those who have been reconciled are now given the work of reconciling. We become messengers of peace, both between people and God, and between people and each other. Every believer has this ministry. Not just pastors or missionaries, but everyone who has been brought back to God. This might look like sharing the good news with a friend, helping two people in conflict find peace, or modelling forgiveness in your family. You have been given a ministry. Look for an opportunity to use it today.
question: Where could you help bring peace between people today?
prayer: Lord, You reconciled me to Yourself through Christ and gave me the ministry of reconciliation. Make me a messenger of peace, and show me where peace is needed today. Amen.

text: To wit, that God was in Christ, reconciling the world unto himself, not imputing their trespasses unto them; and hath committed unto us the word of reconciliation.
reflection: Paul explains the heart of reconciliation in one sentence: "God was in Christ, reconciling the world unto himself, not imputing their trespasses unto them." To impute means to count against, to put on someone's account. Our trespasses deserved to be counted against us. But God chose not to. Instead, as Paul says a few verses later, He made Christ to be sin for us, so that we might be made the righteousness of God in Him. Our sin was placed on Christ's account, and His righteousness was placed on ours. This is the great exchange at the heart of the gospel. Notice also the scope: the world. God's reconciling love is not limited to one people or one kind of person. It reaches everyone. And Paul says God has committed to us the word of reconciliation. We carry this message. It is the best news anyone can hear. God is not counting your sins against you. He has made peace through Christ. Receive it, and share it.
question: Who in your life needs to hear that God is not counting their trespasses against them?
prayer: Lord, You were in Christ, reconciling the world to Yourself and not counting our trespasses. Thank You for this good news. Help me share it with someone today. Amen.

text: But God commendeth his love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us.
reflection: Most people show love to those who deserve it. We love our friends, our family, and those who are kind to us. Paul describes a different kind of love: "But God commendeth his love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us." Commendeth means proves, demonstrates, puts on display. God did not just say He loved us. He showed it in the most costly way possible. And He showed it at the worst possible moment. Not after we cleaned up our lives. Not when we were seeking Him. While we were yet sinners. While we were still rebelling. That is the nature of grace. It is not a reward for good behaviour. It is love given to the undeserving. If you ever doubt that God loves you, look at this verse. His love was not based on your goodness then, and it is not based on your performance now. It rests on His character. Let that settle deep in your heart today.
question: Where are you still trying to earn God's love by your performance?
prayer: Father, You showed Your love while I was still a sinner. Your love was never a reward for my goodness. Help me rest today in a love I do not have to earn. Amen.

text: For if, when we were enemies, we were reconciled to God by the death of his Son, much more, being reconciled, we shall be saved by his life.
reflection: Paul makes an argument from the greater to the lesser: "For if, when we were enemies, we were reconciled to God by the death of his Son, much more, being reconciled, we shall be saved by his life." Think about what this means. When we were God's enemies, He went to the greatest lengths to reconcile us. Now that we are His friends, will He abandon us? Of course not. If God did the hardest thing for us when we were against Him, He will certainly keep us now that we are His. This verse speaks to anyone who worries about falling away or losing God's love. Your security does not rest on your ability to hold on to God. It rests on His commitment to hold on to you. The same love that reached you as an enemy will keep you as a child. Much more is a phrase of great confidence. Let it calm your fears today. If He reconciled you, He will keep you.
question: What fear could be calmed by knowing your security rests on God's commitment, not your ability?
prayer: Lord, You reconciled me when I was Your enemy; how much more will You keep me now. Let my security rest on Your faithfulness, and calm my fears today. Amen.

text: If thou count me therefore a partner, receive him as myself.
reflection: Philemon is a short letter about a real situation. Onesimus was a slave who had run away from his master, Philemon, and possibly stolen from him. While away, Onesimus met Paul and became a believer. Now Paul was sending him back, and he wrote to ask Philemon to receive him: "If thou count me therefore a partner, receive him as myself." Paul put himself in Onesimus's place. He asked Philemon to treat the runaway as he would treat Paul himself. He even offered to pay whatever Onesimus owed. This is a beautiful picture of what Christ does for us. He stands in our place and asks the Father to receive us as He would receive Him. He pays our debt. And now Paul calls Philemon to extend that same grace to someone who had wronged him. Reconciliation sometimes needs a go-between, someone who will speak for the one who has failed. Could you be that person for someone today? Or could you be the Philemon who receives?
question: Is there someone you could welcome back or speak up for, as Paul did for Onesimus?
prayer: Lord Jesus, You stand in my place and pay my debt before the Father. Make me a peacemaker, and give me a welcoming heart toward someone who needs to be received. Amen.

text: For I will be merciful to their unrighteousness, and their sins and their iniquities will I remember no more.
reflection: Can God forget? He knows everything, so in one sense He cannot. But this verse, quoted in Hebrews from Jeremiah, makes a stunning promise: "For I will be merciful to their unrighteousness, and their sins and their iniquities will I remember no more." When God says He will remember our sins no more, He means He will never bring them up again. He will not hold them against us. He will not treat us as our sins deserve. He chooses not to call them to mind. People often say they forgive but do not forget. They bring up old offences in the next argument. God does not do that. Forgiven sin is truly finished in His sight. This month we have thought about forgiveness from many angles: receiving it from God and extending it to others. End the month by resting in this promise. If God has chosen to remember your sins no more, you can stop rehearsing them too. Walk in the freedom He has given you.
question: How would you walk differently today if you truly believed God remembers your forgiven sins no more?
prayer: Lord, You are merciful to my unrighteousness and remember my sins no more. Thank You for that promise. Help me walk in the freedom You have given me. Amen.
